questions.stem: Gregor Mendel conducted his pioneering genetics experiments on which plant?

options.text: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum)
Garden pea (Pisum sativum)
Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris)
Maize (Zea mays)

questions.explanation: Mendel chose garden pea (Pisum sativum) for his experiments (1856–1863) because of its contrasting heritable traits (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, etc.), short generation time, ability to self-fertilise, and ease of controlled cross-fertilisation. He studied 7 traits in about 29,000 plants. His paper was published in 1866 but largely ignored until its rediscovery in 1900 by de Vries, Correns, and Tschermak.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: In a monohybrid cross between a homozygous tall pea plant (TT) and a dwarf plant (tt), the F1 generation will be:

options.text: All dwarf (tt)
50% tall (Tt) and 50% dwarf (tt)
All tall (Tt)
25% TT, 25% tt, and 50% Tt

questions.explanation: When TT × tt, all F1 offspring receive one T allele from the tall parent and one t allele from the dwarf parent, giving 100% Tt (heterozygous). Since T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf), all F1 plants are phenotypically tall. The 3:1 ratio (3 tall : 1 dwarf) appears only in the F2 generation when F1 plants are self-fertilised: TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1 genotype; 3 tall:1 dwarf phenotype.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Mendel's Law of Segregation states that:

options.text: During gamete formation, the two alleles of a gene separate so that each gamete carries only one allele for each trait
Genes on different chromosomes are inherited independently of each other
Dominant alleles always completely mask recessive alleles in phenotype
Alleles acquired during an organism's lifetime can be passed to offspring

questions.explanation: The Law of Segregation (Mendel's First Law) states that each diploid organism has two alleles for each gene, and these alleles separate (segregate) during meiosis so each gamete receives only one allele. This is why a Tt plant produces equal numbers of T and t gametes. The molecular basis is the separation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I. Mendel's Second Law (Independent Assortment) describes genes on different chromosomes assorted independently.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A person with the genotype IAIB will have which blood group?

options.text: Blood group A
Blood group B
Blood group O
Blood group AB

questions.explanation: In the ABO blood group system, IA and IB are codominant alleles — both are fully expressed simultaneously. A person with IAIB genotype expresses both A and B antigens on their red blood cells and has Blood Group AB. This is a classic example of codominance, distinct from incomplete dominance (where an intermediate phenotype appears). Blood group O requires the ii genotype. IA is dominant over i; IB is dominant over i.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. A carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) marries a normal man (XᴴY). What fraction of their sons are expected to be haemophilic?

options.text: 50% (1 in 2 sons)
25% (1 in 4 children overall)
100% (all sons)
0% (sons cannot be haemophilic if father is normal)

questions.explanation: Cross: XᴴXʰ (carrier mother) × XᴴY (normal father). Gametes from mother: Xᴴ or Xʰ; from father: Xᴴ or Y. Possible sons: XᴴY (normal) and XʰY (haemophilic) in equal proportions. So 50% of sons will be haemophilic. Overall, 1/4 of all children will be haemophilic sons. Queen Victoria was a famous carrier of haemophilia A, spreading it to European royal families.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A 'test cross' in genetics is performed by crossing an individual of unknown genotype with:

options.text: The individual's sibling to check for recessive disorders
A heterozygous individual for the same trait
A homozygous recessive individual, so offspring ratios reveal the unknown genotype
An unrelated individual from a different population

questions.explanation: A test cross involves crossing the organism of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive individual (tt). If the unknown is homozygous dominant (TT), all offspring will be Tt (phenotypically dominant). If the unknown is heterozygous (Tt), half the offspring will be Tt (dominant) and half tt (recessive). The offspring phenotype ratio reveals the unknown parent's genotype. Mendel used this technique to verify his predictions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The double helix structure of DNA was described in the landmark paper published in 1953 by:

options.text: Gregor Mendel and Hugo de Vries
James Watson and Francis Crick
Erwin Chargaff and Linus Pauling
Frederick Griffith and Oswald Avery

questions.explanation: Watson and Crick published their DNA double helix model in Nature (April 1953), based on: (1) Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling's X-ray crystallography data ('Photo 51'); (2) Chargaff's rules (A=T, G=C base pairing); (3) Pauling's alpha-helix protein model as inspiration. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (1962). Franklin, who died in 1958, was not included.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A DNA sample contains 20% adenine (A). According to Chargaff's rules, what is the percentage of guanine (G) in this sample?
questions.explanation: Chargaff's rules: A = T and G = C (complementary base pairing). Given A = 20%, then T = 20%. Total A + T = 40%. Since A+T+G+C = 100%, G+C = 60%. Since G = C, G = 30%. **Short trick:** In a DNA double strand: A+G = T+C = 50% of total bases. Given A=20%, T=20%; G+C=60%, so G=C=30%.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Incomplete dominance (as in snapdragon flower colour) differs from codominance (as in ABO blood groups) in that:

options.text: In incomplete dominance, one allele is completely dominant and the other is completely recessive
Codominance is found only in plants while incomplete dominance is found only in animals
In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype (blending); in codominance, both alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed
They are actually the same phenomenon with different names

questions.explanation: Incomplete dominance: Red × White snapdragon → Pink F1 (heterozygote is intermediate). F2 ratio: 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White (1:2:1 phenotypic). Codominance: IAIB blood group — both IA and IB antigens are fully expressed on red blood cells, not blended. AB blood is not 'intermediate'; it has both A and B antigens. Both result in 1:2:1 phenotypic F2 ratios but the heterozygous phenotype differs.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) results from:

options.text: A deletion on the short arm of chromosome 21
A translocation between chromosomes 14 and 21
A point mutation in a gene on chromosome 21
Non-disjunction during meiosis, producing a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21 so the offspring has three copies (47 chromosomes total)

questions.explanation: Most Down syndrome cases (95%) result from trisomy 21 — non-disjunction during meiosis I (most commonly in the mother's egg cell) produces a gamete with two chromosome-21 copies. When fertilised, the resulting zygote has three copies (47 chromosomes). Risk increases with maternal age. Other forms include Robertsonian translocation (4%) and mosaic Down syndrome (1%). Features: intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, increased Alzheimer risk later in life.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a specific point mutation in the β-globin gene. This mutation changes which amino acid at position 6 of the β-globin chain?

options.text: Glutamic acid → Valine, causing HbS haemoglobin to polymerize under low oxygen, distorting red blood cells into a sickle shape
Valine → Glutamic acid, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of haemoglobin
Lysine → Proline, affecting the tertiary structure of the globin chain
Alanine → Glycine, making the red blood cells more fragile but not sickle-shaped

questions.explanation: Sickle cell anaemia results from a single nucleotide change (GAG → GTG) in the 6th codon of β-globin, replacing glutamic acid (hydrophilic) with valine (hydrophobic). HbS (sickle haemoglobin) polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape, causing haemolysis, vaso-occlusion, and pain crises. Heterozygotes (HbA/HbS) have sickle cell trait — mild symptoms but increased malaria resistance, explaining the allele's high frequency in malaria-endemic regions.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) was developed by:

options.text: Frederick Sanger (who developed DNA sequencing)
Kary Mullis, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993
Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen (founders of recombinant DNA technology)
James Watson and Francis Crick

questions.explanation: PCR was invented by Kary Mullis in 1983 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1993). PCR amplifies small DNA segments using: (1) denaturation (heating to ~95°C separates strands); (2) annealing (cooling to ~55–65°C for primers to bind); (3) extension (DNA polymerase synthesises new strands at ~72°C). The use of thermostable Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus) made PCR practical. Applications: forensics, medical diagnosis, paternity testing, research.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross (between AABB × aabb parents) arises because of:

options.text: Incomplete dominance in both genes simultaneously
Linkage — the two genes are on the same chromosome and inherited together
Codominance of both gene pairs
The Law of Independent Assortment — two genes on different chromosomes assort independently, giving 4 gamete types in equal proportion from AaBb F1 parents

questions.explanation: When F1 (AaBb) self-fertilises: each parent produces 4 gamete types in equal ratio (AB:Ab:aB:ab = 1:1:1:1) because the two genes on different chromosomes assort independently. Crossing 4×4 gametes in a Punnett square gives 16 combinations: 9 A_B_ (dominant for both) : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb. This 9:3:3:1 ratio is the hallmark of a dihybrid cross following Mendel's Second Law.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) arises from:

options.text: A deletion on the Y chromosome eliminating male-determining genes
A point mutation in the SRY (sex-determining region Y) gene
Non-disjunction during meiosis producing either an XX egg or an XY sperm, resulting in a zygote with two X chromosomes and one Y
Exposure to excess oestrogen during foetal development

questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) results from non-disjunction: either (a) non-disjunction in the mother's egg produces an XX egg that is fertilised by Y sperm → XXY; or (b) non-disjunction in the father produces an XY sperm that fertilises a normal X egg → XXY. Phenotype: genetically male, infertile (small testes), tall with long limbs, gynaecomastia (breast development), often reduced testosterone. Turner syndrome (45,X) involves monosomy X — one fewer sex chromosome.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Dolly the sheep — the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell — was created in 1996 at which institution?

options.text: Harvard University, USA
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, USA
Tokyo University, Japan
The Roslin Institute, Scotland, UK, by Ian Wilmut and colleagues using somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT)

questions.explanation: Dolly was created at the Roslin Institute (Edinburgh, Scotland) by Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell, and colleagues in 1996 (announced 1997). She was cloned by somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT): the nucleus from a mammary gland cell of a 6-year-old ewe was inserted into an enucleated egg cell, which developed into Dolly. Dolly lived to age 6 (half the normal sheep lifespan), raised concerns about premature ageing in clones. She was named after Dolly Parton.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Bt cotton — India's first genetically modified crop, approved for commercial cultivation in 2002 — contains genes from which organism?

options.text: Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium; its Cry proteins are toxic to bollworm and other Lepidopteran larvae
A wild relative of cotton (Gossypium arboreum) with natural pest resistance
Rhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen and improve plant growth
Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which promotes faster root development

questions.explanation: Bt cotton carries genes from Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), a naturally occurring soil bacterium. The cry (crystal protein) genes encode Cry proteins (specifically Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab in most Indian Bt cotton varieties) that are toxic to bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) larvae when ingested. This reduces the need for pesticide sprays targeting bollworm. Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the vector used to introduce genes into plants (not the source of the insecticidal gene).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Genes that are located on the same chromosome are called 'linked genes'. Which process allows linked alleles to be separated and produces new allele combinations?

options.text: Mitosis — cell division during growth separates linked alleles
Translation — ribosome reading separates mRNA codons from their paired alleles
Crossing over (recombination) — exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes during Prophase I of meiosis
DNA replication errors during S phase of the cell cycle

questions.explanation: During Prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) and may exchange segments at points called chiasmata — this is crossing over (recombination). Crossing over separates linked alleles that would otherwise always travel together, producing recombinant chromosomes with new allele combinations. The frequency of crossing over between two loci is used to construct genetic maps (Morgan's work on chromosome mapping in Drosophila).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Turner syndrome is characterised by which karyotype and phenotype?

options.text: 47,XXX — triple X female with mild or no clinical effects
45,X — monosomy X; phenotypically female but with ovarian dysgenesis, short stature, webbed neck, and absent secondary sexual characteristics
47,XXY — male phenotype with small testes and gynaecomastia
46,XY with SRY gene mutation — genetically male but phenotypically female (androgen insensitivity)

questions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X or 45,X0) involves monosomy X — only one X chromosome instead of two (45 chromosomes total). Affected individuals are phenotypically female but have: ovarian dysgenesis (streak gonads → infertility), short stature, webbed neck (pterygium colli), broad chest, coarctation of aorta, and primary amenorrhoea. Klinefelter (47,XXY) is the male equivalent. Turner syndrome affects ~1 in 2,500 live female births.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A father has blood group A (IAi genotype) and a mother has blood group B (IBi genotype). What blood groups are possible in their children?

options.text: Only A and B — they cannot have AB or O children
Only AB — codominance always produces AB in this cross
A, B, AB, and O — all four blood groups are possible
Only O — both parents carry the i recessive allele, which dominates

questions.explanation: Father (IAi) × Mother (IBi): Gametes from father = IA or i; gametes from mother = IB or i. Four possible offspring genotypes: IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B), ii (O). So all four blood groups are possible with equal probability (25% each). **Short trick:** Whenever both parents carry a hidden recessive 'i' allele (blood groups A or B with IAi or IBi), blood group O children are possible.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The molecular basis of Mendel's Law of Segregation is the:

options.text: Independent assortment of non-homologous chromosomes during metaphase I of meiosis
Exchange of DNA between sister chromatids during S phase of mitosis
Mutation of one allele to match the other during DNA replication
Separation of homologous chromosomes (bearing the two alleles of a gene) during Anaphase I of meiosis, ensuring each gamete gets only one allele

questions.explanation: The molecular/cellular basis of segregation: before meiosis begins, each chromosome is replicated. Homologous chromosomes (e.g., one carrying T, one carrying t) pair up in Prophase I. During Anaphase I, homologs separate to opposite poles — each primary cell gets one chromosome from each homologous pair. After meiosis II, each gamete has one allele (either T or t). This is the physical realisation of Mendel's abstract law, confirmed after chromosomes were recognised as the carriers of hereditary material.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A woman has normal vision but her father was colour-blind (X-linked recessive). She marries a colour-blind man. What is the probability that their first son will be colour-blind?

options.text: 0% — sons cannot be colour-blind if the mother has normal vision

questions.explanation: Since the woman's father was colour-blind (Xᶜ Y), she must have received Xᶜ from him. With normal vision, she is a carrier: Xᴺ Xᶜ. Her husband is colour-blind: Xᶜ Y. Cross for sons: they receive Y from father and either Xᴺ or Xᶜ from mother. Sons: 50% Xᴺ Y (normal vision) and 50% Xᶜ Y (colour-blind). Therefore, 50% of sons will be colour-blind. **Short trick:** Sons get their X only from the mother; if she's a carrier, half her sons get the faulty allele.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The ABO blood group gene has three alleles (IA, IB, i) — an example of multiple allelism. Any individual, however, carries at most two alleles. Which genotype combination correctly proves that blood group O requires BOTH alleles to be the recessive i allele?

options.text: Blood group O individuals are always ii genotype; IAi gives blood group A, IBi gives blood group B, IAIB gives AB — demonstrating that the O antigen (encoded by i) appears only when no dominant allele is present
Blood group O can also result from IAIB by a regulatory mechanism that silences both antigens
Blood group O individuals can be IAi if there is incomplete penetrance of the IA allele
Blood group O is determined by the H antigen gene, completely independent of the ABO gene

questions.explanation: The i allele encodes a non-functional glycosyltransferase, so no A or B antigen is added to the H antigen on red blood cells → blood group O. Because IA and IB are both dominant over i, only the homozygous ii genotype produces blood group O. IAi → A (IA dominant over i); IBi → B; IAIB → AB (codominance). The Bombay phenotype (hh) is a separate rare condition where the H antigen itself is absent — not the same as blood group O from ii genotype.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The X-ray crystallography image 'Photo 51', crucial to Watson and Crick's DNA model, was taken by:

options.text: Linus Pauling at Caltech, USA
Erwin Chargaff at Columbia University, USA
Rosalind Franklin (and Raymond Gosling) at King's College London
Maurice Wilkins working independently of Franklin at King's College London

questions.explanation: Photo 51 was taken by Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling at King's College London in May 1952. It clearly showed the helical structure and the dimensions of DNA. Maurice Wilkins (at the same institution) showed this photograph to Watson without Franklin's knowledge. Watson and Crick used it, along with Chargaff's base-pairing rules, to build their double helix model. Franklin's critical contribution was not acknowledged in the Nobel Prize citation.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: A diploid cell (2n=46) has just completed S phase (DNA replication) but has NOT yet undergone any cell division. The cell now has:

options.text: 92 chromosomes with 92 chromatids
46 chromosomes, each consisting of 2 sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids total — but still 46 centromeres
23 chromosomes (the cell has begun to reduce its chromosome number for meiosis)
46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids (no change from before S phase)

questions.explanation: After S phase (DNA replication), each chromosome consists of 2 identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. The chromosome number remains 46 (diploid), but each chromosome is now a bichromatid structure. Total chromatid count = 46 × 2 = 92. The number of centromeres = 46. Chromosome number only reduces when centromeres separate (in Anaphase II of meiosis or Anaphase of mitosis). Counting chromatids vs chromosomes vs centromeres is a frequent exam point.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Rh incompatibility (erythroblastosis fetalis) during pregnancy typically occurs when:

options.text: The father is Rh-negative and the mother is Rh-positive; their Rh gene difference causes placental dysfunction
An Rh-positive mother develops antibodies against her Rh-negative fetus's red blood cells
Both parents are Rh-negative but a mutation causes the first fetus to become Rh-positive
An Rh-negative mother sensitised during a first Rh-positive pregnancy develops anti-Rh IgG antibodies that, in a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy, cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells

questions.explanation: Rh incompatibility develops over multiple pregnancies: (1st pregnancy) Rh-negative mother carries Rh-positive fetus; at delivery, fetal RBCs enter maternal circulation and she makes anti-Rh antibodies — but the first baby is usually unaffected. (2nd+ Rh-positive pregnancies) IgG anti-Rh antibodies (formed in the 1st pregnancy) cross the placenta and haemolyse fetal RBCs → haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN). Prevention: Rh-negative mothers are given anti-D immunoglobulin (Rhogam) after delivery of Rh+ babies.
